impact.stocks: The S&P 500 fell 0.4% in the last cash session, to 7,561.67. The Dow rose 0.1%, the Nasdaq fell 0.9%, and the Russell 2000 fell 0.3%. Over the 5 sessions in this window, the S&P 500 rose 2.5%. The Nasdaq lagged the S&P 500, so the technology-heavy end of the market was weaker than the broad list. For a long-term investor, one session changes the price of a diversified holding today. It does not, by itself, change the earnings that holding can collect over many years.
impact.rates: The U.S. 10-year yield finished at 5.15%. It rose 5 basis points on the session and 29 basis points over 5 sessions. Alongside it: the 5-year at 4.98%, the 30-year at 5.48%, and the 13-week bill at 4.12%. The 10-year yield sits about 103 basis points above the 13-week bill, so longer-term money costs more than very short-term money. Higher yields raise the return available on plain government bonds and the hurdle stock valuations are measured against. Borrowing costs that follow Treasury yields face upward pressure. Companies whose profits are expected further in the future are usually more sensitive to that hurdle than businesses that earn their cash sooner.
impact.risk: The VIX, a gauge of expected S&P 500 volatility, is 19.30, and it rose 3.2% on the session. Over 5 sessions it fell 24.7%. That is a moderate reading, neither unusually calm nor a stress spike. WTI crude fell 0.2% to $88.56, gold was little changed at $3,886.30, and the U.S. dollar index rose 0.2% to 103.41. The newest headlines cluster around artificial intelligence, monetary policy, inflation, energy prices, geopolitics and trade, and earnings and new listings. Taken together, index moves, the Treasury yield, and volatility describe the backdrop. They are context for risk, not a signal to trade.
